arXiv:1509.07127v3 [quant-ph] 07 Aug 2018

Universal recovery maps and approximate sufficiency of quantum relative entropy

Marius Junge Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Illinois 61801-2975, USA    Renato Renner Affiliation: Institute for Theoretical Physics, ETH Zurich, Switzerland    David Sutter Affiliation: Institute for Theoretical Physics, ETH Zurich, Switzerland    Mark M. Wilde Affiliation: Hearne Institute for Theoretical Physics, Department of Physics and Astronomy, Center for Computation and Technology, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, Louisiana 70803, USA    Andreas Winter Affiliation: ICREA & Física Teòrica: Informació i Fenòmens Quàntics, Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona, ES-08193 Bellaterra (Barcelona), Spain.
Abstract

The data processing inequality states that the quantum relative entropy between two states ρ\rho and σ\sigma can never increase by applying the same quantum channel 𝒩\mathcal{N} to both states. This inequality can be strengthened with a remainder term in the form of a distance between ρ\rho and the closest recovered state (ℛ∘𝒩)​(ρ)(\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho), where ℛ\mathcal{R} is a recovery map with the property that σ=(ℛ∘𝒩)​(σ)\sigma=(\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{N})(\sigma). We show the existence of an explicit recovery map that is universal in the sense that it depends only on σ\sigma and the quantum channel 𝒩\mathcal{N} to be reversed. This result gives an alternate, information-theoretic characterization of the conditions for approximate quantum error correction.

1 Introduction

For two Hilbert spaces AA and BB, let S⁡(A)\mathrm{S}(A) denote the set of density operators on AA and let TPCP⁡(A,B)\mathrm{TPCP}(A,B) be the set of trace-preserving completely positive maps from AA to BB.11 1 A linear mapping 𝒩A→B\mathcal{N}_{A\to B} from AA to BB is said to be completely positive if (𝒩A→B⊗ℐR)​(ρA​R)≥0(\mathcal{N}_{A\to B}\otimes\mathcal{I}_{R})(\rho_{AR})\geq 0 for all ρA​R≥0\rho_{AR}\geq 0, where RR denotes an arbitrary reference system and ℐR\mathcal{I}_{R} denotes the identity map on RR. The mapping is additionally trace preserving if any positive semi-definite trace-class input operator is mapped to an output operator that has the same trace. Let Q⁡(A)\mathrm{Q}(A) denote some subset of S⁡(A)\mathrm{S}(A). A quantum channel 𝒩∈TPCP⁡(A,B)\mathcal{N}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(A,B) is called sufficient (or reversible) with respect to Q⁡(A)\mathrm{Q}(A), if there exists a recovery map ℛ∈TPCP⁡(B,A)\mathcal{R}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(B,A) such that

(ℛ∘𝒩)​(ρ)=ρfor allρ∈Q⁡(A).\displaystyle(\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho)=\rho\quad\textnormal{for all}\quad\rho\in\mathrm{Q}(A)\ . (1)

Sufficiency of quantum channels has been studied extensively (see [29, 30, 26, 16] and references therein).

The quantum relative entropy between two states ρ\rho and σ\sigma is defined as [22]

D(ρ∥σ):=∑i⟨ϕi|ρ(logρ−logσ)|ϕi⟩=∑i,j|⟨ϕi|ψj⟩|2[p(i)logp(i)−p(i)logq(j)],\displaystyle D(\rho\|\sigma):=\sum_{i}\langle\phi_{i}|\rho(\log\rho-\log\sigma)|\phi_{i}\rangle=\sum_{i,j}|\langle\phi_{i}|\psi_{j}\rangle|^{2}[p(i)\log p(i)-p(i)\log q(j)]\,, (2)

where ρ=∑ip⁡(i)​|ϕi⟩​⟨ϕi|\rho=\sum_{i}p(i)|\phi_{i}\rangle\langle\phi_{i}| and σ=∑jq⁡(j)​|ψj⟩​⟨ψj|\sigma=\sum_{j}q(j)|\psi_{j}\rangle\langle\psi_{j}| are spectral decompositions of ρ\rho and σ\sigma with {|ϕi⟩}i\{|\phi_{i}\rangle\}_{i} and {|ψj⟩}j\{|\psi_{j}\rangle\}_{j} orthonormal bases. Note that if the support of ρ\rho is not contained in the support of σ\sigma, then D(ρ∥σ)=+∞D(\rho\|\sigma)=+\infty. The data processing inequality (also known as monotonicity of the relative entropy) states that D(ρ∥σ)D(\rho\|\sigma) is non-increasing under trace-preserving completely positive maps [24, 41], i.e.,

D(ρ∥σ)≥D(𝒩(ρ)∥𝒩(σ)),\displaystyle D(\rho\|\sigma)\geq D(\mathcal{N}(\rho)\|\mathcal{N}(\sigma))\,, (3)

where 𝒩\mathcal{N} is a quantum channel. The data processing inequality is related to the sufficiency of 𝒩\mathcal{N}. As shown in [29, 30, 16, 17], a quantum channel 𝒩∈TPCP⁡(A,B)\mathcal{N}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(A,B) is sufficient with respect to Q⁡(A)\mathrm{Q}(A) if and only if D(ρ∥σ)=D(𝒩(ρ)∥𝒩(σ))D(\rho\|\sigma)=D(\mathcal{N}(\rho)\|\mathcal{N}(\sigma)) for all ρ∈Q⁡(A)\rho\in\mathrm{Q}(A) and σ∈Q⁡(A)\sigma\in\mathrm{Q}(A). It is known that this is the case if and only if there exists a recovery map ℛ∈TPCP⁡(B,A)\mathcal{R}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(B,A) that simultaneously reverses the action of the physical evolution 𝒩\mathcal{N} on both states [29, 30, 31], i.e., (ℛ∘𝒩)​(ρ)=ρ(\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho)=\rho and (ℛ∘𝒩)​(σ)=σ(\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{N})(\sigma)=\sigma.

Let L⁡(B)\mathrm{L}(B) denote the set of bounded operators on BB, TC⁡(A)\mathrm{TC}(A) the set of trace-class operators on AA, and 𝒩†\mathcal{N}^{\dagger} the adjoint map of 𝒩\mathcal{N}.22 2 Note that the adjoint 𝒩†\mathcal{N}^{\dagger} of 𝒩\mathcal{N} is defined as the unique linear map satisfying ⟨a,𝒩†​(b)⟩=⟨𝒩⁡(a),b⟩\left\langle a,\mathcal{N}^{\dagger}(b)\right\rangle=\left\langle\mathcal{N}(a),b\right\rangle for all a∈TC⁡(A)a\in\mathrm{TC}(A) and b∈L⁡(B)b\in\mathrm{L}(B), where ⟨a1,a2⟩:=tr⁡(a1†​a2)\left\langle a_{1},a_{2}\right\rangle:=\mathrm{tr}(a_{1}^{\dagger}a_{2}) is the Frobenius inner product. We consider ⟨a1,a2⟩ω:=tr⁡(a1†​ω12​a2​ω12)\left\langle a_{1},a_{2}\right\rangle_{\omega}:=\mathrm{tr}(a_{1}^{\dagger}\omega^{\frac{1}{2}}a_{2}\omega^{\frac{1}{2}}), which is an inner product on the space of operators {a∈L⁡(A):Πω​a=a​Πω=a}\{a\in\mathrm{L}(A)\,:\,\Pi_{\omega}a=a\Pi_{\omega}=a\}, where Πω\Pi_{\omega} is the projection onto the support of ω\omega. If the Hilbert spaces AA and BB are assumed to be separable and σ∈TC⁡(A)\sigma\in\mathrm{TC}(A) is positive semi-definite, then the recovery map can be taken as the Petz recovery map 𝒫σ,𝒩\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}} (also known as the transpose map), defined as the adjoint of the solution to

⟨a,𝒩†​(b)⟩σ=⟨𝒫σ,𝒩†​(a),b⟩𝒩⁡(σ)​Êfor alla∈L⁡(A),b∈L⁡(B).\displaystyle\langle a,\mathcal{N}^{\dagger}(b)\rangle_{\sigma}=\langle\mathcal{P}^{\dagger}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}(a),b\rangle_{\mathcal{N}(\sigma)}Ê\quad\textnormal{for all}\quad a\in\mathrm{L}(A),b\in\mathrm{L}(B)\ . (4)

The Petz recovery map 𝒫σ,𝒩\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}} is completely positive, trace non-increasing and unique on the support of 𝒩⁡(σ)\mathcal{N}(\sigma) [29, 30, 31, 28]. In the case that the Hilbert spaces AA and BB are finite-dimensional, then, on the support of 𝒩⁡(σ)\mathcal{N}(\sigma), the Petz recovery map takes the form

𝒫σ,𝒩:XB↦σ12​𝒩†​(𝒩​(σ)−12​XB​𝒩​(σ)−12)​σ12.\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}\ :\ X_{B}\mapsto\sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathcal{N}^{\dagger}\bigl(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)^{-\frac{1}{2}}X_{B}\,\mathcal{N}(\sigma)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\bigr)\sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}\ . (5)

(Following the standard convention, σ−1\sigma^{-1} is defined to be the inverse of σ\sigma on its support.)

The concept of sufficient statistics can be made robust. For ε∈[0,1]\varepsilon\in[0,1], a quantum channel 𝒩∈TPCP⁡(A,B)\mathcal{N}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(A,B) is ε\varepsilon-sufficient with respect to Q⁡(A)\mathrm{Q}(A) if there exists a recovery map ℛε∈TPCP⁡(B,A)\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(B,A) such that [15]

12​‖ρ−(ℛε∘𝒩)​(ρ)‖1≤εfor allρ∈Q⁡(A).\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\rho-(\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho)\right\rVert_{1}\leq\varepsilon\quad\textnormal{for all}\quad\rho\in\mathrm{Q}(A)\,. (6)

Together with the case ε=0\varepsilon=0 discussed above and ideas from [44], this motivates the question if there exists a stronger version of the data processing inequality. More precisely, one asks for the possibility of adding a non-negative term to the right-hand side of (3) that indicates how well ρ\rho can be recovered from 𝒩⁡(ρ)\mathcal{N}(\rho). Such a relation would serve as an alternative characterization of approximate sufficient statistics.

An inequality that is closely related to the monotonicity of the relative entropy is the strong subadditivity of quantum entropy [20, 21], which ensures that for any tripartite state ρA​B​C∈S⁡(A⊗B⊗C)\rho_{ABC}\in\mathrm{S}(A\otimes B\otimes C) the conditional mutual information is non-negative, i.e., I(A:C|B)ρ:=H(AB)ρ+H(BC)ρ−H(ABC)ρ−H(B)ρ≥0I(A:C|B)_{\rho}:=H(AB)_{\rho}+H(BC)_{\rho}-H(ABC)_{\rho}-H(B)_{\rho}\geq 0, where H​(A)ρ:=−tr⁡(ρA​log⁡ρA)H(A)_{\rho}:=-\mathrm{tr}(\rho_{A}\log\rho_{A}) denotes the von Neumann entropy.33 3 The definition of conditional mutual information we have given is for finite-dimensional spaces and can be extended to the infinite-dimensional case [36]. This inequality has been strengthened recently with a remainder term in the form of a distance to the closest recovered state. It was shown in [8], that for any density operator ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC}, there exists ℛB→B​C∈TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C) (the recovery map) such that

I(A:C|B)ρ≥−2logF(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C(ρA​B)),\displaystyle I(A:C|B)_{\rho}\geq-2\log F(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB}))\ , (7)

where the fidelity of ρ\rho and σ\sigma is defined by [40]

F⁡(ρ,σ):=‖ρ​σ‖1.\displaystyle F(\rho,\sigma):=\left\lVert\sqrt{\rho}\sqrt{\sigma}\right\rVert_{1}\,. (8)

If AA, BB, and CC are finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, on the support of ρB\rho_{B}, ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} can be taken as a rotated Petz recovery map, i.e., a trace-preserving completely positive map of the form

XB↦VB​C​ρB​C12​(ρB−12​UB​XB​UB†​ρB−12⊗idC)​ρB​C12​VB​C†,\displaystyle X_{B}\mapsto V_{BC}\rho_{BC}^{\frac{1}{2}}(\rho_{B}^{-\frac{1}{2}}U_{B}X_{B}U_{B}^{\dagger}\rho_{B}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{C})\rho_{BC}^{\frac{1}{2}}V_{BC}^{\dagger}\ , (9)

where VB​CV_{BC} and UBU_{B} are unitaries on B⊗CB\otimes C and BB, respectively.

The result of [8], whose proof is based on de Finetti type arguments and properties of Rényi entropies, has been extended and generalized in various ways. In [6], based on the quantum state redistribution protocol [7] and de Finetti type arguments, it was shown that the fidelity term can be replaced by a measured relative entropy D𝕄D_{\mathbb{M}}, which is never smaller than the fidelity term, i.e.,

I(A:C|B)ρ≥D𝕄(ρA​B​C∥ℛB→B​C(ρA​B))≥−2logF(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C(ρA​B)).\displaystyle I(A:C|B)_{\rho}\geq D_{\mathbb{M}}(\rho_{ABC}\|\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB}))\geq-2\log F(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB}))\ . (10)

The measured relative entropy is defined as the supremum of the relative entropy with measured inputs over all positive operator-valued measures (POVMs) ℳ={Mx}\mathcal{M}=\{M_{x}\}, i.e.,

D𝕄(ρ∥σ):=sup{D(ℳ(ρ)∥ℳ(σ)):ℳ(ρ)=∑xtr(ρMx)|x⟩⟨x| with ∑xMx=id},\displaystyle D_{\mathbb{M}}(\rho\|\sigma):=\sup\Bigl\{D\bigl(\mathcal{M}(\rho)\big\|\mathcal{M}(\sigma)\bigr):\mathcal{M}(\rho)=\sum_{x}\mathrm{tr}(\rho M_{x})|x\rangle\!\langle x|\text{ with }\sum_{x}M_{x}=\mathrm{id}\Bigr\}\ , (11)

where {|x⟩}x\{|x\rangle\}_{x} is a finite set of orthonormal vectors. We note that the tighter bound from [6] came at the cost of losing all information about the structure of the recovery map. In [38], it was shown that there exists a recovery map both satisfying (10) and possessing a universality property, in the sense that it only depends on the marginal ρB​C\rho_{BC}. Furthermore, for a linearized version of (7) it was shown that the recovery map has the form of a rotated Petz recovery map with commuting unitaries, i.e., a recovery map of the form in (9) where VB​CV_{BC} and UBU_{B} commute with ρB​C\rho_{BC} and ρB\rho_{B}, respectively.

In view of approximate sufficiency of quantum channels discussed above, it would be helpful to have a generalization of (7) in terms of relative entropies. This has been established in [42] with a proof technique based on the notion of a Rényi generalization of a relative entropy difference [35] and Hadamard’s three-line theorem. It was shown that for any two states ρ\rho and σ\sigma on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces with supp⁡(ρ)⊆supp⁡(σ)\mathrm{supp}(\rho)\subseteq\mathrm{supp}(\sigma) and any channel 𝒩\mathcal{N} there exists a recovery map ℛ\mathcal{R} such that (ℛ∘𝒩)​(σ)=σ(\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{N})(\sigma)=\sigma and

D(ρ∥σ)−D(𝒩(ρ)∥𝒩(σ))≥−2logF(ρ,(ℛ∘𝒩)(ρ)).\displaystyle D(\rho\|\sigma)-D\bigl(\mathcal{N}(\rho)\|\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\bigr)\geq-2\log F\bigl(\rho,(\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho)\bigr)\ . (12)

Furthermore, the recovery map was shown to be a rotated Petz recovery map with unitaries UU and VV in the algebra generated by σ\sigma and 𝒩⁡(σ)\mathcal{N}(\sigma), respectively. Very recently, another different proof technique was found [39], based on the concavity and monotonicity of the operator logarithm, which shows that there exists a recovery map ℛ\mathcal{R} such that

D(ρ∥σ)−D(𝒩(ρ)∥𝒩(σ))\displaystyle D(\rho\|\sigma)-D\bigl(\mathcal{N}(\rho)\|\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\bigr) ≥D𝕄(ρ∥(ℛ∘𝒩)(ρ))\displaystyle\geq D_{\mathbb{M}}\bigl(\rho\|(\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho)\bigr) (13)
≥−2​log⁡F⁡(ρ,(ℛ∘𝒩)​(ρ)).\displaystyle\geq-2\log F\bigl(\rho,(\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho)\bigr)\ . (14)

The recovery map was shown to be a convex combination of rotated Petz recovery maps with unitaries UU and VV in the algebra generated by σ\sigma and 𝒩⁡(σ)\mathcal{N}(\sigma), respectively, and therefore satisfies (ℛ∘𝒩)​(σ)=σ(\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{N})(\sigma)=\sigma.

Neither in [42] nor in [39] could the recovery map satisfying (12) and (13), respectively, be shown to be universal, in the sense that it could be taken independent of ρ\rho. We note that by the Fuchs-van de Graaf inequality [9] the fidelity can be transferred into a trace distance term such that (12) and (14) provide alternative characterizations for approximate sufficient statistics.

Result.

We show that for any non-negative operator σ\sigma and for any channel 𝒩\mathcal{N} there exists an explicit and universal recovery map ℛσ,𝒩\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}} such that

D(ρ∥σ)≥D(𝒩(ρ)∥𝒩(σ))−2logF(ρ,(ℛσ,𝒩∘𝒩)(ρ))\displaystyle D(\rho\|\sigma)\geq D\bigl(\mathcal{N}(\rho)\|\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\bigr)-2\log F\bigl(\rho,(\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho)\bigr) (15)

for all density operators ρ\rho such that supp⁡(ρ)⊆supp⁡(σ)\mathrm{supp}(\rho)\subseteq\mathrm{supp}(\sigma). A consequence of the universality of the recovery map ℛσ,𝒩\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}} is that (ℛσ,𝒩∘𝒩)​(σ)=σ(\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\sigma)=\sigma. We note that ρ\rho and σ\sigma are defined on separable Hilbert spaces. We refer to Theorem 2.1 and Remark 2.2 for a more precise statement, and we note here that the result stated in Theorem 2.1 is strictly stronger than (15).

History of the problem.

In 1973, the strong subadditivity of quantum entropy [20, 21] was proven. It ensures that the conditional mutual information of any tripartite state is non-negative. Two years later the data processing inequality, or monotonicity of the quantum relative entropy under trace-preserving completely positive maps was proven [24, 41]. This entropy inequality states that the quantum relative entropy cannot increase after applying a quantum channel to its arguments. Since then it has been realized that this fundamental theorem has numerous applications in quantum physics, and as a consequence, it was natural to ask if it would be possible to strengthen the result. This however turned out to be challenging. More recently, several conjectures regarding an improved data processing inequality have been put forward. (See [44] for one of these conjectures). In this paper, we prove (15) with a recovery map that satisfies all the properties that have been conjectured to hold (see e.g., [44]).

2 Main results

Let P⁡(A)\mathrm{P}(A) denote the set of non-negative trace-class operators on a Hilbert space AA. For any σ∈P⁡(A)\sigma\in\mathrm{P}(A), we define

Sσ​(A):={ρ∈S⁡(A):supp⁡(ρ)⊆supp⁡(σ)}.\displaystyle\mathrm{S}_{\sigma}(A):=\{\rho\in\mathrm{S}(A):\mathrm{supp}(\rho)\subseteq\mathrm{supp}(\sigma)\}\ . (16)
Theorem 2.1.

Let AA and BB be separable Hilbert spaces. For any σ∈P⁡(A)\sigma\in\mathrm{P}(A), any ρ∈Sσ​(A)\rho\in\mathrm{S}_{\sigma}(A) and any 𝒩∈TPCP⁡(A,B)\mathcal{N}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(A,B) we have

D(ρ||σ)≥D(𝒩(ρ)||𝒩(σ))−2∫ℝdtβ0(t)logF(ρ,(ℛσ,𝒩t2∘𝒩)(ρ)),\displaystyle D(\rho|\hskip-1.13809pt|\sigma)\geq D\bigl(\mathcal{N}(\rho)|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\bigr)-2\int_{\mathbb{R}}\mathrm{d}t\,\beta_{0}(t)\,\log F\bigl(\rho,(\mathcal{R}^{\frac{t}{2}}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho)\bigr)\ , (17)

where the relative entropy and fidelity are defined in (2) and (8), respectively. The recovery map is given by

ℛσ,𝒩t:XB↦σ−i​t​𝒫σ,𝒩​(𝒩​(σ)i​t​XB​𝒩​(σ)−i​t)​σi​t\displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{t}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}:X_{B}\mapsto\sigma^{-\mathrm{i}t}\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}\bigl(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)^{\mathrm{i}t}X_{B}\,\mathcal{N}(\sigma)^{-\mathrm{i}t}\bigr)\sigma^{\mathrm{i}t} (18)

and β0\beta_{0} a probability density function on ℝ\mathbb{R} defined by

β0​(t):=π2​(cosh⁡(π​t)+1)−1.\displaystyle\beta_{0}(t):=\frac{\pi}{2}\bigl(\cosh(\pi t)+1\bigr)^{-1}\ . (19)

The map 𝒫σ,𝒩\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}} is the Petz recovery map, defined as the adjoint of the unique linear map 𝒫σ,𝒩†\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}^{{\dagger}} satisfying (4) with domain L⁡(supp⁡(𝒩⁡(σ)))\mathrm{L}(\mathrm{supp}(\mathcal{N}(\sigma))) and range L⁡(supp⁡(σ))\mathrm{L}(\mathrm{supp}(\sigma)). If AA and BB are finite-dimensional, this unique linear map 𝒫σ,𝒩\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}} is given by (5).

Remark 2.2.

Using the concavity of the logarithm and the fidelity [27, Exercise 9.20], Theorem 2.1 can be simplified to

D(ρ||σ)≥D(𝒩(ρ)||𝒩(σ))−2logF(ρ,(ℛσ,𝒩∘𝒩)(ρ)),\displaystyle D(\rho|\hskip-1.13809pt|\sigma)\geq D\bigl(\mathcal{N}(\rho)|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\bigr)-2\log F\bigl(\rho,(\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho)\bigr)\ , (20)

where

ℛσ,𝒩​(⋅):=∫ℝd​t​β0​(t)​ℛσ,𝒩t2​(⋅)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}(\cdot):=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\mathrm{d}t\,\beta_{0}(t)\,\mathcal{R}^{\frac{t}{2}}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}(\cdot) (21)

on the support of 𝒩⁡(σ)\mathcal{N}(\sigma) with ℛσ,𝒩t\mathcal{R}^{t}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}} and β0\beta_{0} defined in Theorem 2.1.44 4 The integral in (21) can be understood as a Riemann sum with respect to weak convergence since we have a weakly continuous family of maps.

Figure 1 depicts the probability density β0\beta_{0} as a function of t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}. We note that the recovery map ℛσ,𝒩\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}} that satisfies (20) can be chosen such that it projects everything outside of the support of 𝒩⁡(σ)\mathcal{N}(\sigma) to zero.

Remark 2.3.

Inequality (17) together with the fact that the mapping t↦ℛσ,𝒩tt\mapsto\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}^{t} is continuous implies that for any σ∈P⁡(A)\sigma\in\mathrm{P}(A), ρ∈Sσ​(A)\rho\in\mathrm{S}_{\sigma}(A) and 𝒩∈TPCP⁡(A,B)\mathcal{N}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(A,B) such that D(ρ∥σ)=D(𝒩(ρ)∥𝒩(σ))D(\rho\|\sigma)=D(\mathcal{N}(\rho)\|\mathcal{N}(\sigma)) we have (ℛσ,𝒩t∘𝒩)​(ρ)=ρ(\mathcal{R}^{t}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho)=\rho and (ℛσ,𝒩t∘𝒩)​(σ)=σ(\mathcal{R}^{t}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\sigma)=\sigma for all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} with ℛσ,𝒩t​(⋅)\mathcal{R}^{t}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}(\cdot) defined in (18). This follows because F⁡(ω,τ)∈[0,1]F(\omega,\tau)\in[0,1] and F⁡(ω,τ)=1F(\omega,\tau)=1 if and only if ω=τ\omega=\tau for density operators ω\omega and τ\tau.

Remark 2.4 (Functoriality properties).

The recovery map ℛσ,𝒩\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}} stated in Remark 2.2 satisfies apart from (20) several desirable “functoriality” properties. Some of them have been stated in [44, 19, 42].

  1. 1.

    Universality. The recovery map does not depend on ρ\rho. This follows directly from Remark 2.2.

  2. 2.

    Perfect reconstruction of σ\sigma from 𝒩⁡(σ)\mathcal{N}(\sigma). The recovery map satisfies (ℛσ,𝒩∘𝒩)​(σ)=σ(\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\sigma)=\sigma. This is clear from the fact that any rotated Petz map of the form in (18) perfectly recovers σ\sigma [42], and thus so does any convex combination of these maps. Alternatively, as the recovery map predicted by Remark 2.2 that satisfies (20) is universal, the assertion follows by choosing ρ=σ/tr⁡(σ)\rho=\sigma/\mathrm{tr}(\sigma).

  3. 3.

    Normalization. In case 𝒩=ℐ\mathcal{N}=\mathcal{I}, where ℐ\mathcal{I} denotes the identity map, we have ℛσ,𝒩​(⋅)=Πσ​(⋅)​Πσ\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}(\cdot)=\Pi_{\sigma}(\cdot)\Pi_{\sigma}, where Πσ\Pi_{\sigma} denotes a projector onto the support of σ\sigma. Thus if σ\sigma is faithful the recovery map is equal to the identity channel. This follows directly by [42, Section 4.1] and by definition of the recovery map ℛσ,𝒩​(⋅)\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}(\cdot).

  4. 4.

    Stabilization. For any σ∈P⁡(A)\sigma\in\mathrm{P}(A), any 𝒩∈TPCP⁡(A,B)\mathcal{N}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(A,B), any reference system RR, and any faithful τ∈P⁡(R)\tau\in\mathrm{P}(R), we have ℛσ⊗τ,𝒩⊗ℐR​(⋅)=ℛσ,𝒩⊗ℐR​(⋅)\mathcal{R}_{\sigma\otimes\tau,\mathcal{N}\otimes\mathcal{I}_{R}}(\cdot)=\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}\otimes\mathcal{I}_{R}(\cdot). This follows by combining [42, Section 4.2] together with the normalization property discussed above.

We note that by following [42, Sections 4.2 and 4.3] it can be shown that the recovery map ℛσ,𝒩\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}} fulfills some parallel and serial composition rules.

The proof of Theorem 2.1 consists of two parts. We first prove the statement for finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces AA and BB by employing a strengthened version of Hadamard’s three-line theorem that is due to Hirschman [13]. By an approximation argument we show that the result remains valid for separable Hilbert spaces.

3 Proof of Theorem 2.1

Step 1:Proof for finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces

In this step we assume that the Hilbert spaces AA and BB are finite-dimensional. Our proof of (17) is similar to the approach taken in [42]. There are two main ingredients: a Rényi generalization of a relative entropy difference [35] and Hirschman’s improvement of the Hadamard three-line theorem [13]. We begin by recalling these two ingredients and then proceed to a proof of (17).

Remark 3.4.

If AA and BB are finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces the statement in Remark 2.2 can be slightly generalized. For any σ≥0\sigma\geq 0 and any trace non-increasing completely positive map 𝒩\mathcal{N} with Kraus operators {Ni}\{N_{i}\} such that 0≠∑iNi†​Ni≤id0\neq\sum_{i}N_{i}^{\dagger}N_{i}\leq\mathrm{id} the recovery map ℛσ,𝒩\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}} defined in Remark 2.2 satisfies (20) for all subnormalized density operators ρ≥0\rho\geq 0 with 0<tr⁡(ρ)≤10<\mathrm{tr}(\rho)\leq 1 such that supp⁡(ρ)⊆supp⁡(σ)\mathrm{supp}(\rho)\subseteq\mathrm{supp}(\sigma). This follows by the same argument given in Step 1 by using UA→B​E=∑iNi⊗|i⟩EU_{A\rightarrow BE}=\sum_{i}N_{i}\otimes|i\rangle_{E} as an extension of the trace non-increasing and completely positive map 𝒩\mathcal{N}.

Step 2:Extension to infinite dimensions

In this step the Hilbert spaces AA and BB are assumed to be separable (not necessarily finite-dimensional). We will show how to lift Theorem 2.1 for finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, such that it can apply to states ρ\rho and σ\sigma and a channel 𝒩\mathcal{N} associated with separable Hilbert spaces. This is accomplished via a limiting argument where we consider projected sequences that are finite-dimensional and therefore satisfy the desired inequality. In the limit we then obtain the statement for separable Hilbert spaces. This is a rather standard approach for generalizing statements proven for finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces to separable Hilbert spaces.

Let {ΠAa}a∈ℕ\{\Pi^{a}_{A}\}_{a\in\mathbb{N}} and {ΠBb}b∈ℕ\{\Pi^{b}_{B}\}_{b\in\mathbb{N}} be sequences of finite-rank projectors on AA and BB, respectively, that converge to idA\mathrm{id}_{A} and idB\mathrm{id}_{B}, respectively, with respect to the weak operator topology, meaning that

lima→∞⟨ψ|ΠAa|ϕ⟩=⟨ψ|ϕ⟩\lim_{a\to\infty}\langle\psi|\Pi^{a}_{A}|\phi\rangle=\langle\psi|\phi\rangle (38)

for all vectors |ϕ⟩,|ψ⟩∈A|\phi\rangle,|\psi\rangle\in A (similarly for ΠBb→idB\Pi^{b}_{B}\to\mathrm{id}_{B}). For σ∈P⁡(A)\sigma\in\mathrm{P}(A) and ρ∈Sσ​(A)\rho\in\mathrm{S}_{\sigma}(A) we consider projected versions

σa:=ΠAa​σ​ΠAaandρa:=ΠAa​ρ​ΠAa.\displaystyle\sigma^{a}:=\Pi_{A}^{a}\,\sigma\,\Pi_{A}^{a}\quad\textnormal{and}\quad\rho^{a}:=\Pi_{A}^{a}\,\rho\,\Pi_{A}^{a}\ . (39)

We note that the sequences {ρa}a∈ℕ\{\rho^{a}\}_{a\in\mathbb{N}} and {σa​Ê}a∈ℕ\{\sigma^{a}Ê\}_{a\in\mathbb{N}} converge to ρ\rho and σ\sigma, respectively, in the trace norm (see, e.g., [11] or Lemma 11.1 of [14]). Let Sa\mathrm{S}^{a} be the set of non-negative operators that is generated by (39) for all ρ∈S⁡(A)\rho\in\mathrm{S}(A). For any 𝒩∈TPCP⁡(A,B)\mathcal{N}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(A,B) we define its analogue with a projection at the input and output as

𝒩a,b​(⋅):=ΠBb​𝒩​(ΠAa​(⋅)​ΠAa)​ΠBb.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}^{a,b}(\cdot):=\Pi_{B}^{b}\mathcal{N}\bigl(\Pi_{A}^{a}(\cdot)\Pi_{A}^{a}\bigr)\Pi_{B}^{b}\ . (40)

Note that by combining Grümm’s theorem [37, Theorem 2.19] with the boundedness of 𝒩\mathcal{N} in the trace norm implies that 𝒩a,b\mathcal{N}^{a,b} converges to 𝒩\mathcal{N} in the strong operator topology, i.e.,

lima,b→∞‖𝒩a,b​(ω)−𝒩⁡(ω)‖1=0\lim_{a,b\to\infty}\left\lVert\mathcal{N}^{a,b}(\omega)-\mathcal{N}(\omega)\right\rVert_{1}=0 (41)

for all ω∈TC⁡(A)\omega\in\mathrm{TC}(A).

We start by proving two lemmas that show how the difference of relative entropies and the fidelity, respectively, change when considering projected states.

Lemma 3.5.

For any σ∈P⁡(A)\sigma\in\mathrm{P}(A), any ρ∈Sσ​(A)\rho\in\mathrm{S}_{\sigma}(A), and any 𝒩∈TPCP⁡(A,B)\mathcal{N}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(A,B), we have

lima→∞D(ρa∥σa)=D(ρ∥σ)\displaystyle\lim_{a\to\infty}D(\rho^{a}\|\sigma^{a})=D(\rho\|\sigma) (42)

and

lim infa→∞lim infb→∞D(𝒩a,b(ρa)∥𝒩a,b(σa))≥D(𝒩(ρ)∥𝒩(σ)).\displaystyle\liminf_{a\to\infty}\liminf_{b\to\infty}D\bigl(\mathcal{N}^{a,b}(\rho^{a})\big\|\,\mathcal{N}^{a,b}(\sigma^{a})\bigr)\geq D\bigl(\mathcal{N}(\rho)\big\|\,\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\bigr)\ . (43)
Proof.

Recall that Lindblad defined a relative entropy (which slightly differs from our definition of the relative entropy) for two positive trace class operators τ\tau and ω\omega as

D¯(τ∥ω):=∑j⟨j|(τlogτ−τlogω+ω−τ)|j⟩=D(τ∥ω)+tr(ω)−tr(τ),\displaystyle\bar{D}(\tau\|\omega):=\sum_{j}\langle j|\left(\tau\log\tau-\tau\log\omega+\omega-\tau\right)|j\rangle=D(\tau\|\omega)+\mathrm{tr}(\omega)-\mathrm{tr}(\tau)\,, (44)

where {|j⟩}\{|j\rangle\} is a complete orthonormal set of eigenvectors of τ\tau or ω\omega. By Lemma 3 in [23] we have

D(ρa∥σa)\displaystyle D(\rho^{a}\|\sigma^{a}) =D¯(ρa∥σa)+tr(ρa)−tr(σa)\displaystyle=\bar{D}(\rho^{a}\|\sigma^{a})+\mathrm{tr}(\rho^{a})-\mathrm{tr}(\sigma^{a}) (45)
≤D¯(ρ∥σ)+tr(ρa)−tr(σa)\displaystyle\leq\bar{D}(\rho\|\sigma)+\mathrm{tr}(\rho^{a})-\mathrm{tr}(\sigma^{a}) (46)
=D(ρ∥σ)+tr(ρa−ρ)+tr(σ−σa).\displaystyle=D(\rho\|\sigma)+\mathrm{tr}(\rho^{a}-\rho)+\mathrm{tr}(\sigma-\sigma^{a})\,. (47)

Since the relative entropy is lower semicontinuous [14, Theorem 11.6], we obtain

D(ρ∥σ)≤lim infa→∞D(ρa∥σa).D(\rho\|\sigma)\leq\liminf_{a\to\infty}D(\rho^{a}\|\sigma^{a})\ . (48)

Combining these shows that

lima→∞D(ρa∥σa)=D(ρ∥σ).\displaystyle\lim_{a\to\infty}D(\rho^{a}\|\sigma^{a})=D(\rho\|\sigma)\ . (49)

The lower semicontinuity of the relative entropy implies that

lim infa→∞lim infb→∞D(𝒩a,b(ρa)∥𝒩a,b(σa))\displaystyle\liminf_{a\to\infty}\liminf_{b\to\infty}D\bigl(\mathcal{N}^{a,b}(\rho^{a})\|\mathcal{N}^{a,b}(\sigma^{a})\bigr) ≥lim infa→∞D(𝒩(ρa)∥𝒩(σa))\displaystyle\geq\liminf_{a\to\infty}D\bigl(\mathcal{N}(\rho^{a})\|\mathcal{N}(\sigma^{a})\bigr) (50)
≥D(𝒩(ρ)∥𝒩(σ)).\displaystyle\geq D\bigl(\mathcal{N}(\rho)\|\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\bigr)\ . (51)

This proves the assertion. ∎

Lemma 3.6.

The Petz recovery map 𝒫σa,𝒩a,b\mathcal{P}_{\sigma^{a},\mathcal{N}^{a,b}} defined in (5) satisfies lima→∞limb→∞𝒫σa,𝒩a,b=𝒫σ,𝒩\lim_{a\to\infty}\lim_{b\to\infty}\mathcal{P}_{\sigma^{a},\mathcal{N}^{a,b}}=\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}, where 𝒫σ,𝒩\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}} is a recovery map that is defined as the (unique) linear map with domain supp⁡(𝒩⁡(σ))\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)) and range supp⁡(σ)\operatorname{supp}(\sigma) satisfying

⟨a2,𝒩†​(a1)⟩σ=⟨𝒫σ,𝒩†​(a2),a1⟩𝒩⁡(σ)​Êfor alla1∈L⁡(B),a2∈L⁡(A),\displaystyle\left\langle a_{2},\mathcal{N}^{\dagger}(a_{1})\right\rangle_{\sigma}=\left\langle\mathcal{P}^{\dagger}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}(a_{2}),a_{1}\right\rangle_{\mathcal{N}(\sigma)}Ê\quad\textnormal{for all}\quad a_{1}\in\mathrm{L}(B),\,a_{2}\in\mathrm{L}(A)\ , (52)

with the weighted inner product ⟨a,b⟩ω:=tr⁡(a†​ω12​b​ω12)\left\langle a,b\right\rangle_{\omega}:=\mathrm{tr}(a^{\dagger}\omega^{\frac{1}{2}}b\omega^{\frac{1}{2}}) and ω\omega positive semi-definite and trace class.

Proof.

We begin by outlining the proof. As shown by Petz [29, 30, 31] (see also [28, Chapter 8]), the map 𝒫σa,𝒩a,b\mathcal{P}_{\sigma^{a},\mathcal{N}^{a,b}} defined in (5) is the unique linear map with domain supp⁡(𝒩a,b​(σa))\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{N}^{a,b}(\sigma^{a})) and range supp⁡(σa)\operatorname{supp}(\sigma^{a}) satisfying

and the map 𝒫σ,𝒩\mathcal{P}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}} is the unique linear map with domain supp⁡(𝒩⁡(σ))\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)) and range supp⁡(σ)\operatorname{supp}(\sigma) satisfying

Before stating the following lemma, we introduce the shorthand

𝒰ω,t:X↦ωi​t​X​ω−i​t,\mathcal{U}_{\omega,t}:X\mapsto\omega^{\mathrm{i}t}X\omega^{-\mathrm{i}t}\ , (79)

where ω\omega is a positive semi-definite operator.

Lemma 3.7.

For any σ∈P⁡(A)\sigma\in\mathrm{P}(A), any ρ∈Sσ​(A)\rho\in\mathrm{S}_{\sigma}(A), any 𝒩∈TPCP⁡(A,B)\mathcal{N}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(A,B), and all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, the following limit holds

lima→∞limb→∞F⁡(ρa,(ℛσa,𝒩a,bt∘𝒩a,b)​(ρa))=F⁡(ρ,(ℛσ,𝒩t∘𝒩)​(ρ)).\displaystyle\lim_{a\to\infty}\lim_{b\to\infty}F\bigl(\rho^{a},(\mathcal{R}^{t}_{\sigma^{a},\mathcal{N}^{a,b}}\circ\mathcal{N}^{a,b})(\rho^{a})\bigr)=F\bigl(\rho,(\mathcal{R}^{t}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho)\bigr)\,. (80)
Proof.

We start with a reminder of a standard result: let ω\omega and {ωn}n∈ℕ\{\omega_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} be positive semi-definite trace-class operators such that limn→∞‖ωn−ω‖1=0\lim_{n\to\infty}\left\lVert\omega_{n}-\omega\right\rVert_{1}=0. Then, for any t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} and any bounded linear operator XX the term ωni​t​X​ωn−i​t\omega_{n}^{\mathrm{i}t}X\omega_{n}^{-\mathrm{i}t} converges to ωi​t​X​ω−Ê​i​t\omega^{\mathrm{i}t}X\omega^{-Ê\mathrm{i}t} for n→∞n\to\infty in the weak operator topology. To see this we note that by Cauchy-Schwarz we have

|⟨φ,(ωni​t​X​ωn−i​t−ωi​t​X​ω−i​t)​ϕ⟩|\displaystyle\left|\langle\varphi,(\omega_{n}^{\mathrm{i}t}X\omega_{n}^{-\mathrm{i}t}-\omega^{\mathrm{i}t}X\omega^{-\mathrm{i}t})\phi\rangle\right|
=|⟨φ,(ωni​t​X​ωn−i​t−ωni​t​X​ω−i​t)+(ωni​t​X​ω−i​t−ωi​t​X​ω−i​t)​ϕ⟩|\displaystyle=\left|\langle\varphi,(\omega_{n}^{\mathrm{i}t}X\omega_{n}^{-\mathrm{i}t}-\omega_{n}^{\mathrm{i}t}X\omega^{-\mathrm{i}t})+(\omega_{n}^{\mathrm{i}t}X\omega^{-\mathrm{i}t}-\omega^{\mathrm{i}t}X\omega^{-\mathrm{i}t})\phi\rangle\right| (81)
≤|⟨X​ωn−i​t​φ,(ωn−i​t−ω−i​t)​ϕ⟩|+|⟨(ωni​t−ωi​t)​φ,X​ω−i​t​ϕ⟩|\displaystyle\leq\left|\langle X\omega_{n}^{-\mathrm{i}t}\varphi,(\omega_{n}^{-\mathrm{i}t}-\omega^{-\mathrm{i}t})\phi\rangle\right|+\left|\langle(\omega_{n}^{\mathrm{i}t}-\omega^{\mathrm{i}t})\varphi,X\omega^{-\mathrm{i}t}\phi\rangle\right| (82)
≤‖X‖​‖φ‖​‖(ωn−i​t−ω−i​t)​ϕ‖+‖X‖​‖ϕ‖​‖(ωni​t−ωi​t)​φ‖.\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert X\right\rVert\left\lVert\varphi\right\rVert\left\lVert(\omega_{n}^{-\mathrm{i}t}-\omega^{-\mathrm{i}t})\phi\right\rVert+\left\lVert X\right\rVert\left\lVert\phi\right\rVert\left\lVert(\omega_{n}^{\mathrm{i}t}-\omega^{\mathrm{i}t})\varphi\right\rVert\,. (83)

We first note that for any fixed k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}

limn→∞‖(Πk​ωn−i​t​Πk−Πk​ω−i​t​Πk)​ϕ‖=0.\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\left\lVert(\Pi_{k}\omega_{n}^{-\mathrm{i}t}\Pi_{k}-\Pi_{k}\omega^{-\mathrm{i}t}\Pi_{k})\phi\right\rVert=0\,. (84)

To see this we recall Duhamel’s formula which shows that

(Πk​ωn−i​t​Πk−Πk​ω−i​t​Πk)\displaystyle\!\!\!\!(\Pi_{k}\omega_{n}^{-\mathrm{i}t}\Pi_{k}-\Pi_{k}\omega^{-\mathrm{i}t}\Pi_{k})
=(e−i​t​log⁡Πk​ωn​Πk−e−i​t​log⁡Πk​ω​Πk)\displaystyle=(\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}t\log\Pi_{k}\omega_{n}\Pi_{k}}-\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}t\log\Pi_{k}\omega\Pi_{k}}) (85)
=i​∫0td​s​e−i​s​log⁡Πk​ωn​Πk​(log⁡Πk​ω​Πk−log⁡Πk​ωn​Πk)​e−i⁡(t−s)​log⁡Πk​ω​Πk.\displaystyle=\mathrm{i}\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{d}s\,\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}s\log\Pi_{k}\omega_{n}\Pi_{k}}(\log\Pi_{k}\omega\Pi_{k}-\log\Pi_{k}\omega_{n}\Pi_{k})\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}(t-s)\log\Pi_{k}\omega\Pi_{k}}\,. (86)

Theorem X.3.7 from [5] ensures that for any fixed k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}

This proves the assertion. ∎

4 Universal and explicit refinements of other entropy inequalities

It is well known (see e.g. [34]) that the monotonicity of the relative entropy under trace-preserving completely positive maps is closely related to (i) strong subadditivity, (ii) concavity of the conditional entropy, and (iii) joint convexity of the relative entropy. Based on this relation, Remark 2.2 can be used to derive universal and explicit remainder terms for the statements (i)-(iii). We note that universal means that the recovery map that occurs in the remainder term does not depend on all possible parameters. Within this section we assume that AA, BB, and CC are finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. For n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, the nn-simplex is denoted by Δn:={x∈ℝn:x≥0,∑i=1nxi=1}\Delta_{n}:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\ x\geq 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}=1\}.

Applying Remark 2.2 for σ=idA⊗ρB​C∈P⁡(A⊗B⊗C)\sigma=\mathrm{id}_{A}\otimes\rho_{BC}\in\mathrm{P}(A\otimes B\otimes C), ρ=ρA​B​C∈Sσ​(A⊗B⊗C)\rho=\rho_{ABC}\in\mathrm{S}_{\sigma}(A\otimes B\otimes C), and 𝒩A​B​C→A​B=ℐA​B⊗trC\mathcal{N}_{ABC\to AB}=\mathcal{I}_{AB}\otimes\mathrm{tr}_{C} implies a strengthened version of the result that has been established in [38, Theorem 2.1, Corollary 2.4, and Remark 2.5].

Corollary 4.1 (Strong subadditivity).

For any density operator ρA​B​C∈S⁡(A⊗B⊗C)\rho_{ABC}\in\mathrm{S}(A\otimes B\otimes C) we have

I(A:C|B)ρ≥−2logF(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C(ρA​B)),\displaystyle I(A:C|B)_{\rho}\geq-2\log F\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)\ , (101)

where ℛB→B​C​(⋅)=∫ℝd​t​β0​(t)​ℛρB​C,trCt​(⋅)\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\cdot)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\mathrm{d}t\beta_{0}(t)\mathcal{R}^{t}_{\rho_{BC},\mathrm{tr}_{C}}(\cdot) as defined in Theorem 2.1.

From Corollary 4.1 we can deduce a universal remainder term for the concavity of the conditional entropy. We note that a similar remainder term has been conjectured in [4]. Furthermore, a remainder term that however is neither universal nor explicit has been proven in [42, Corollary 12].

Corollary 4.2 (Concavity of conditional entropy).

For any ρA​B∈S⁡(A⊗B)\rho_{AB}\in\mathrm{S}(A\otimes B) we have

H(A|B)ρ−∑x∈𝒳ν(x)H(A|B)ρx≥−2log∑x∈𝒳ν(x)F(ρA​Bx,ℛB→A​B(ρBx)),\displaystyle H(A|B)_{\rho}-\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\nu(x)H(A|B)_{\rho^{x}}\geq-2\log\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\nu(x)F\bigl(\rho_{AB}^{x},\mathcal{R}_{B\to AB}(\rho_{B}^{x})\bigr)\ , (102)

for all ensembles {ν⁡(x),ρA​Bx}x∈𝒳\{\nu(x),\rho_{AB}^{x}\}_{x\in\mathcal{X}} with ν∈Δ𝒳\nu\in\Delta_{\mathcal{X}} and ρA​Bx∈S⁡(A⊗B)\rho_{AB}^{x}\in\mathrm{S}(A\otimes B) such that ρA​B=∑x∈𝒳ν⁡(x)​ρA​Bx\rho_{AB}=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\nu(x)\rho_{AB}^{x} where ℛB→A​B​(⋅)=∫ℝd​t​β0​(t)​ℛρA​B,trAt​(⋅)\mathcal{R}_{B\to AB}(\cdot)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\mathrm{d}t\beta_{0}(t)\mathcal{R}^{t}_{\rho_{AB},\mathrm{tr}_{A}}(\cdot) as defined in Theorem 2.1.

Proof.

Let us consider the following classical-quantum state

ϕX​A​B=∑x∈𝒳ν⁡(x)​|x⟩​⟨x|X⊗ρA​Bx.\displaystyle\phi_{XAB}=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\nu(x)|x\rangle\!\langle x|_{X}\otimes\rho_{AB}^{x}\ . (103)

By Corollary 4.1 and a simple fact ensuring that the fidelity for orthogonal input states decomposes (see Lemma A.1 in [38]), we find

H​(A|B)ρ−∑x∈𝒳ν⁡(x)​H​(A|B)ρx\displaystyle H(A|B)_{\rho}-\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\nu(x)H(A|B)_{\rho^{x}} =H​(A|B)ϕ−H​(A|B​X)ϕ\displaystyle=H(A|B)_{\phi}-H(A|BX)_{\phi} (104)
=I(X:A|B)ϕ\displaystyle=I(X:A|B)_{\phi} (105)
≥−2​log⁡F⁡(ϕX​A​B,ℛB→A​B​(ϕX​B))\displaystyle\geq-2\log F\bigl(\phi_{XAB},\mathcal{R}_{B\to AB}(\phi_{XB})\bigr) (106)
=−2log∑x∈𝒳ν(x)F(ρA​Bx,ℛB→A​B(ρBx)).\displaystyle=-2\log\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\nu(x)F\bigl(\rho_{AB}^{x},\mathcal{R}_{B\to AB}(\rho_{B}^{x})\bigr)\ . (107)

We note that by Corollary 4.1 the recovery map ℛB→A​B\mathcal{R}_{B\to AB} is explicit and universal in the sense that it only depends on ρA​B\rho_{AB}. ∎

Remark 2.2 implies a universal remainder term for the joint convexity of the relative entropy. We note that a similar remainder term has been conjectured in [35]. Corollary 13 in [42] proves such a remainder term that however is neither universal nor explicit.

Corollary 4.3 (Joint convexity of relative entropy).

For any ν∈Δ𝒳\nu\in\Delta_{\mathcal{X}}, {σx}x∈𝒳\{\sigma^{x}\}_{x\in\mathcal{X}} with σx∈P⁡(A)\sigma^{x}\in\mathrm{P}(A) for all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, σX​A=∑x∈𝒳ν⁡(x)​|x⟩​⟨x|X⊗σx\sigma_{XA}=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\nu(x){|x\rangle\!\langle x|_{X}\otimes\sigma^{x}}, any ρx∈Sσx​(A)\rho_{x}\in\mathrm{S}_{\sigma^{x}}(A) and ρ=∑x∈𝒳ν⁡(x)​ρx\rho=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\nu(x)\rho^{x} we have

∑x∈𝒳ν(x)D(ρx||σx)−D(ρ||σ)≥−2log∑x∈Sν(x)F(ρx,ℛσX​A,trX(ρ)),\displaystyle\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\nu(x)D(\rho^{x}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\sigma^{x})-D(\rho|\hskip-1.13809pt|\sigma)\geq-2\log\sum_{x\in\mathrm{S}}\nu(x)F\bigl(\rho^{x},\mathcal{R}_{\sigma_{XA},\mathrm{tr}_{X}}(\rho)\bigr)\ , (108)

where ℛσX​A,trX​(⋅)=∫ℝd​t​β0​(t)​ℛσX​A,trXt​(⋅)\mathcal{R}_{\sigma_{XA},\mathrm{tr}_{X}}(\cdot)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\mathrm{d}t\beta_{0}(t)\mathcal{R}^{t}_{\sigma_{XA},\mathrm{tr}_{X}}(\cdot) as defined in Theorem 2.1.

Proof.

Let us consider the states

ρX​A:=∑x∈𝒳ν⁡(x)​|x⟩​⟨x|X⊗ρxandρ=ρA=∑x∈𝒳ν⁡(x)​ρx.\displaystyle\rho_{XA}:=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\nu(x)|x\rangle\!\langle x|_{X}\otimes\rho^{x}\quad\textnormal{and}\quad\rho=\rho_{A}=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\nu(x)\rho^{x}\ . (109)

Since the relative entropy decomposes for orthogonal input states (see Lemma B.2 in [38]), Remark 2.2 implies that the recovery map ℛσX​A,trX​(⋅)=∫ℝd​t​β0​(t)​ℛσX​A,trXt​(⋅)\mathcal{R}_{\sigma_{XA},\mathrm{tr}_{X}}(\cdot)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\mathrm{d}t\beta_{0}(t)\mathcal{R}^{t}_{\sigma_{XA},\mathrm{tr}_{X}}(\cdot) satisfies

∑x∈𝒳ν(x)D(ρx||σx)−D(ρ||σ)\displaystyle\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\nu(x)D(\rho^{x}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\sigma^{x})-D(\rho|\hskip-1.13809pt|\sigma) =D(ρX​A||σX​A)−D(ρA||σA)\displaystyle=D(\rho_{XA}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\sigma_{XA})-D(\rho_{A}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\sigma_{A}) (110)
≥−2​log⁡F⁡(ρX​A,ℛσX​A,trX​(ρ))\displaystyle\geq-2\log F\bigl(\rho_{XA},\mathcal{R}_{\sigma_{XA},\mathrm{tr}_{X}}(\rho)\bigr) (111)
=−2log∑x∈𝒳ν(x)F(ρx,ℛσX​A,trX(ρ)),\displaystyle=-2\log\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\nu(x)F\bigl(\rho^{x},\mathcal{R}_{\sigma_{XA},\mathrm{tr}_{X}}(\rho)\bigr)\ , (112)

where the final step uses that the fidelity for orthogonal input states decomposes (see Lemma A.1 in [38]). ∎

5 Approximate quantum error correction

Theorem 2.1 allows for establishing an alternate, information-theoretic set of conditions for approximate quantum error correction. Recall that in quantum error correction the main goal is to protect a set of states from the action of a noisy quantum channel, by encoding this set into a subspace of a given Hilbert space. The quantum error correction conditions given in the seminal works [3, 18] are necessary and sufficient for perfect quantum error correction. Although these works were essential for gaining an understanding of quantum error correction, the conditions given represent a strong idealization, since we can never hope in practice to have perfect quantum error correction. So this realization motivated some follow-up works on approximate quantum error correction (see [2, 25] and references therein), in which one seeks to determine conditions under which approximate recovery from the action of a given noisy channel is possible. We mention that some of these works made essential use of the Petz recovery map.

In [12], information-theoretic conditions for perfect error correction were given in terms of the quantum relative entropy. We recall their result: Let AA be a Hilbert space, let CC be a subspace of AA (called the “codespace”), and let Π\Pi denote the projection onto CC. Then

{∀ρ∈S(C) : D(ρ∥Π)=D(𝒩(ρ)∥𝒩(Π))}⇔{∀ρ∈S(C) : ρ=(𝒫Π,𝒩∘𝒩)(ρ)},\{\forall\,\rho\in\mathrm{S}(C)\ \textnormal{ : }\ D(\rho\|\Pi)=D(\mathcal{N}(\rho)\|\mathcal{N}(\Pi))\}\iff\{\forall\,\rho\in\mathrm{S}(C)\ \textnormal{ : }\ \rho=(\mathcal{P}_{\Pi,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho)\}\ , (113)

where 𝒫Π,𝒩​(⋅)\mathcal{P}_{\Pi,\mathcal{N}}(\cdot) is the Petz recovery map defined in (5). So perfect error correction is possible if and only if for all ρ∈S⁡(C)\rho\in\mathrm{S}(C) the pairwise distinguishability of ρ\rho with Π\Pi does not decrease under the action of the noisy channel 𝒩\mathcal{N}.

Given the statement in (113) and the prior work on approximate quantum error correction, it is natural to wonder whether a robust version of (113) exists. Indeed, Theorem 2.1 (or rather Remark 2.2) implies such a statement, establishing necessary and sufficient information-theoretic conditions for approximate quantum error correction. Loosely speaking, we can now say that approximate error correction is possible if any only if the pairwise distinguishability of ρ\rho with Π\Pi does not decrease by too much under the action of the noisy channel 𝒩\mathcal{N} for all ρ∈S⁡(C)\rho\in\mathrm{S}(C). The corollary below is a consequence of Remark 2.2 and some other known facts.

Corollary 5.1.

Let ε∈[0,1]\varepsilon\in\left[0,1\right], AA and BB be a finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, CC be a subspace of AA (called the “codespace”), 𝒩∈TPCP⁡(A,B)\mathcal{N}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(A,B) a quantum channel, and let Π\Pi denote the projection onto CC. If for all ρ∈S⁡(C)\rho\in\mathrm{S}(C) we have

D(ρ∥Π)−D(𝒩(ρ)∥𝒩(Π))≤ε,D(\rho\|\Pi)-D\bigl(\mathcal{N}(\rho)\|\mathcal{N}(\Pi)\bigr)\leq\varepsilon\ , (114)

then it is possible to approximately recover every state ρ∈S⁡(C)\rho\in\mathrm{S}(C), in the sense that we have for all ρ∈S⁡(C)\rho\in\mathrm{S}(C)

F⁡(ρ,(ℛΠ,𝒩∘𝒩)​(ρ))≥1−12​ε.F\bigl(\rho,(\mathcal{R}_{\Pi,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho)\bigr)\geq 1-\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon\ . (115)

Conversely, if (115) holds for ε∈[0,1]\varepsilon\in\left[0,1\right], then we have for all ρ∈S⁡(C)\rho\in\mathrm{S}(C)

D(ρ∥Π)−D(𝒩(ρ)∥𝒩(Π))≤εlog(dimC)+h2(ε),D(\rho\|\Pi)-D(\mathcal{N}(\rho)\|\mathcal{N}(\Pi))\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon}\log(\dim C)+h_{2}(\sqrt{\varepsilon})\ , (116)

where h2​(p):=−p​log⁡p−(1−p)​log⁡(1−p)h_{2}(p):=-p\log p-(1-p)\log(1-p) is the binary entropy, with the property that limp↘0h2​(p)=0\lim_{p\searrow 0}h_{2}(p)=0.

Proof.

The first statement is a direct consequence of Remark 2.2, found by setting ρ=ρ\rho=\rho, σ=Π\sigma=\Pi, and 𝒩=𝒩\mathcal{N}=\mathcal{N} and then applying the inequality −log⁡(x)≥1−x-\log(x)\geq 1-x, which holds for x∈[0,1]x\in\left[0,1\right].

To prove the second statement, suppose that (115) holds. By the Fuchs-van-de-Graaf inequality [9], (115) implies that for all ρ∈S⁡(C)\rho\in\mathrm{S}(C) we have

12​‖ρ−(ℛΠ,𝒩∘𝒩)​(ρ)‖1≤ε.\frac{1}{2}\left\|\rho-(\mathcal{R}_{\Pi,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho)\right\|_{1}\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon}\ . (117)

Then consider the following chain of inequalities, which holds for all ρ∈S⁡(C)\rho\in\mathrm{S}(C):

D(ρ∥Π)−D(𝒩(ρ)∥𝒩(Π))\displaystyle\!\!\!\!D(\rho\|\Pi)-D(\mathcal{N}(\rho)\|\mathcal{N}(\Pi))
≤D(ρ∥Π)−D((ℛΠ,𝒩∘𝒩)(ρ)∥(ℛΠ,𝒩∘𝒩)(Π))\displaystyle\leq D(\rho\|\Pi)-D\bigl((\mathcal{R}_{\Pi,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho)\|(\mathcal{R}_{\Pi,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\Pi)\bigr) (118)
=D(ρ∥Π)−D((ℛΠ,𝒩∘𝒩)(ρ)∥Π)\displaystyle=D(\rho\|\Pi)-D\bigl((\mathcal{R}_{\Pi,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho)\|\Pi\bigr) (119)
=−H⁡(ρ)+H⁡((ℛΠ,𝒩∘𝒩)​(ρ))+tr⁡([(ℛΠ,𝒩∘𝒩)​(ρ)−ρ]​log⁡Π)\displaystyle=-H(\rho)+H((\mathcal{R}_{\Pi,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho))+\mathrm{tr}\bigl(\left[(\mathcal{R}_{\Pi,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho)-\rho\right]\log\Pi\bigr) (120)
≤ε​log​dim(C)+h2​(ε).\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon}\log\dim(C)+h_{2}(\sqrt{\varepsilon}). (121)

The first inequality is a consequence of monotonicity of quantum relative entropy with respect to the recovery map ℛΠ,𝒩\mathcal{R}_{\Pi,\mathcal{N}}. The first equality follows because OPEN(ℛΠ,𝒩∘𝒩)​(Π))=Π(\mathcal{R}_{\Pi,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\Pi))=\Pi. The second equality is a rewriting, and the last inequality follows from the Fannes-Audenaert inequality [1] (see also [43, Lemma 1]) and the facts that supp⁡(ρ)⊆supp⁡(Π)\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(\Pi), supp⁡((ℛΠ,𝒩∘𝒩)​(ρ))⊆supp⁡(Π)\operatorname{supp}((\mathcal{R}_{\Pi,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho))\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(\Pi), and log⁡Π=0\log\Pi=0 on the support of Π\Pi. ∎

6 Conclusion

In this work, we showed that for any non-negative operator σ\sigma and for any channel 𝒩\mathcal{N} there exists an explicit and universal recovery map ℛσ,𝒩\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}} such that

D(ρ∥σ)−D(𝒩(ρ)∥𝒩(σ))≥−2logF(ρ,(ℛσ,𝒩∘𝒩)(ρ))\displaystyle D(\rho\|\sigma)-D\bigl(\mathcal{N}(\rho)\|\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\bigr)\geq-2\log F\bigl(\rho,(\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\rho)\bigr) (122)

for all density operators ρ\rho such that supp⁡(ρ)⊆supp⁡(σ)\mathrm{supp}(\rho)\subseteq\mathrm{supp}(\sigma). A consequence of its universality is that the recovery map ℛσ,𝒩\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}} satisfies (ℛσ,𝒩∘𝒩)​(σ)=σ(\mathcal{R}_{\sigma,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\sigma)=\sigma. The present work thus constitutes an improvement over [42] since the recovery map is constructed explicitly and is independent of ρ\rho. Knowing the explicit structure of the recovery map that satisfies (122) can be helpful in various scenarios. For example if this is to be implemented by experimentalists or in an actual quantum computer it is helpful to have an explicit recovery map. We showed that the inequality (122) implies universal and explicit remainder terms for other entropy inequalities such as strong subadditivity, concavity of the entropy, and the joint convexity of the relative entropy. Furthermore, it can be useful in the context of quantum sufficient statistics and approximate quantum error correction.

Appendix

Appendix A Proof of Lemma 3.2

We begin by recalling Hirschman’s strengthening [13] of the Hadamard three-line theorem (see, e.g., [10, Lemma 1.3.8]):

Lemma A.1.

Let S:={z∈ℂ:0≤Re⁡{z}≤1}S:=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}:0\leq\operatorname{Re}\left\{z\right\}\leq 1\right\} and let g⁡(z)g(z) be holomorphic on the interior of SS and continuous on the boundary, such that

supz∈Sexp⁡{−a​|Im⁡z|}​log​|g⁡(z)|≤A<∞,\sup_{z\in S}\exp\left\{-a\left|\operatorname{Im}z\right|\right\}\log\left|g(z)\right|\leq A<\infty, (123)

for some fixed AA and a<πa<\pi. Then for θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1), the following bound holds

log⁡|g⁡(θ)|≤∫ℝd​t​(αθ​(t)​log⁡(|g⁡(i​t)|1−θ)+βθ​(t)​log⁡(|g⁡(1+i​t)|θ)),\log\left|g(\theta)\right|\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}}\mathrm{d}t\ \Bigl(\alpha_{\theta}(t)\log\bigl(\left|g(\mathrm{i}t)\right|^{1-\theta}\bigr)+\beta_{\theta}(t)\log\bigl(\left|g(1+\mathrm{i}t)\right|^{\theta}\bigr)\Bigr), (124)

where αθ​(t)\alpha_{\theta}(t) and βθ​(t)\beta_{\theta}(t) are defined in (28).

We can now prove Lemma 3.2.

Proof of Lemma 3.2.

The proof of this theorem is well known, but we provide it for completeness. For fixed θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1), let qθq_{\theta} be the Hölder conjugate of pθp_{\theta}, defined by

1pθ+1qθ=1.\frac{1}{p_{\theta}}+\frac{1}{q_{\theta}}=1\ . (125)

Similarly, let q0q_{0} and q1q_{1} be Hölder conjugates of p0p_{0} and p1p_{1}, respectively. We can find an operator XX such that

‖X‖qθ=1andtr⁡(X​G​(θ))=‖G⁡(θ)‖pθ.\displaystyle\left\|X\right\|_{q_{\theta}}=1\quad\textnormal{and}\quad\operatorname{tr}(XG(\theta))=\left\|G(\theta)\right\|_{p_{\theta}}\ . (126)

We can write the singular value decomposition for XX in the form X=U​D1/qθ​VX=UD^{1/q_{\theta}}V (implying tr(D)=1(D)=1). For z∈Sz\in S, define

X⁡(z):=U​D1−zq0+zq1​V.X(z):=UD^{\frac{1-z}{q_{0}}+\frac{z}{q_{1}}}V\ . (127)

As a consequence, X⁡(z)X(z) is holomorphic on the interior of SS and continuous on the boundary. Also, observe that X⁡(θ)=XX(\theta)=X. Then the following function satisfies the requirements needed to apply Lemma A.1:

g⁡(z):=tr⁡(X⁡(z)​G​(z)).g(z):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(X(z)G(z)\bigr)\ . (128)

Indeed, we have that

log⁡‖G⁡(θ)‖pθ=log⁡|g⁡(θ)|≤∫ℝd​t​(αθ​(t)​log⁡(|g⁡(i​t)|1−θ)+βθ​(t)​log⁡(|g⁡(1+i​t)|θ)).\log\ \left\|G(\theta)\right\|_{p_{\theta}}=\log\left|g(\theta)\right|\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}}\mathrm{d}t\ \left(\alpha_{\theta}(t)\log\bigl(\left|g(\mathrm{i}t)\right|^{1-\theta}\bigr)+\beta_{\theta}(t)\log\bigl(\left|g(1+\mathrm{i}t)\right|^{\theta}\bigr)\right). (129)

Now, from applying Hölder’s inequality and the facts that ‖X⁡(i​t)‖q0=1=‖X⁡(1+i​t)‖q1\left\|X(it)\right\|_{q_{0}}=1=\left\|X(1+\mathrm{i}t)\right\|_{q_{1}}, we find that

|g⁡(i​t)|\displaystyle\left|g(\mathrm{i}t)\right| =|tr⁡(X⁡(i​t)​G​(i​t))|≤‖X⁡(i​t)‖q0​‖G⁡(i​t)‖p0=‖G⁡(i​t)‖p0\displaystyle=\left|\operatorname{tr}\bigl(X(\mathrm{i}t)G(\mathrm{i}t)\bigr)\right|\leq\left\|X(\mathrm{i}t)\right\|_{q_{0}}\left\|G(\mathrm{i}t)\right\|_{p_{0}}=\left\|G(\mathrm{i}t)\right\|_{p_{0}} (130)

and

|g⁡(1+i​t)|\displaystyle\left|g(1+\mathrm{i}t)\right| =|tr(X(1+it)G(1+it))|≤‖X(1+it)‖q1‖G(1+it)‖p1=‖G(1+it)‖p1.\displaystyle=\left|\operatorname{tr}\bigr(X(1+\mathrm{i}t)G(1+\mathrm{i}t)\bigr)\right|\leq\left\|X(1+\mathrm{i}t)\right\|_{q_{1}}\left\|G(1+\mathrm{i}t)\right\|_{p_{1}}=\left\|G(1+\mathrm{i}t)\right\|_{p_{1}}. (131)

Bounding (129) from above using these inequalities then gives (27). ∎
